newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Richardson to visit 10 nations in Asia, Europe.
newsitem.headline: Richardson to visit 10 nations in Asia, Europe.

text.p: Bill Richardson, the chief U.S. delegate to the United Nations, leaves next week for a two-week trip to 10 nations, mainly to lobby for lowering U.S. dues in the world body, U.S. officials said on Thursday.
The trip, beginning on Monday, will include South Korea, Japan, China, Tajikistan, Kazakstan, Uzbekistan, Georgia, Ukraine, Russia and a quick stop in France.
Richardson said the main issues discussed in South Korea, Japan and China will be U.N. subjects such as Washington's debt to the world body and reform of the Security Council.
In France a major subject will be African issues, such training peacekeeping forces in the continent.

"If our reform agenda is to be successful in New York, we must explain and receive international backing for our initiatives -- to streamline U.N. operations, change the scale of member state assessments and reform the Security Council," Richardson told reporters.

His visit to central Asian republics of the former Soviet Union was requested by U.S. Vice President Al Gore to "enhance our bilateral ties" and discuss the intractable civil war in Afghanistan, he said. In Georgia and Tajikistan, the United Nations has a small peacekeeping operation.

Richardson said he was visiting the Ukraine because its foreign minister, Hennady Udovenko, will be president of the 52nd General Assembly, beginning in September, where the reform issues will be discussed and possibly put to a vote.
Congress is considering paying $819 million in U.S. arrears for peacekeeping, regular dues and voluntary contributions to U.N. agencies, about half of what the United States owes the world body.
But the funds are conditional upon many issues that require approval of the 185-member General Assembly, including lowering of U.S. assessments and making arrangements to forgive the debt.

Many governments currently financing the United Nations, including Japan, Germany and other Europeans, oppose a reduction in U.S. payments until the arrears issues is settled. And China, which is assessed at a low rate, opposes having its dues raised.
"They are arguing that half a loaf is better than no loaf but we are not so sure," said one European envoy.

Security Council reform is equally difficult with the United States having given the process a boost by supporting permanent seats on the 15-member body for three developing countries as well as Germany and Japan.

But unspoken was whether Washington believed the new members should have veto power over council decisions. Officials said only that the U.S. veto, currently also wielded by China, Russia, Britain and France "should not be diluted."
Behind the scenes, Washington as well as other permanent members, are reluctant to give veto power to Third World nations, a stand which could kill council reform.

At the same time the developing countries are far apart in choosing which nations should become permanent members, a situation that complicates setting up the structure of an expanded council before any states are chosen.
The current five permanent council members were the principle Second World War victors and have held their seats since the founding of the United Nations in 1945.
